entry: Region of southern [[Italy]] (pop., 2026: 5,568,703), capital [[Naples]]. Its area is 13,670.95 sq km (5,278 sq mi), and it is the most economically productive region in southern Italy by GDP. The region has 10 of the 58 UNESCO sites in Italy, including [[Pompeii]] and Herculaneum, and [[Mount Vesuvius]] is part of the UNESCO World Network of Biosphere Reserves. The Romans knew it as *Campania felix* ("fertile countryside").

Family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the order *Asterales*, also called the bellflower family. It contains nearly 2,400 species in 84 genera, mostly herbaceous plants with some shrubs and rarely small trees, often with milky sap. Familiar garden plants include *Campanula* (bellflower), *Lobelia* and *Platycodon* (balloonflower). Most current classifications place the family *Lobeliaceae* within it as subfamily Lobelioideae. The family is almost cosmopolitan, occurring on all continents except [[Antarctica]], and [[Hawaii]] is particularly rich, with well over 100 endemic species of Hawaiian lobelioids. Habitats range from extreme deserts to rainforests, and from the tropics to the high [[Arctic]].

[[Pop art]] series of 32 paintings by American artist [[Andy Warhol]]. Each painting depicts a different variety of Campbell's soup cans in a uniform 20-by-16-inch format, and the series was produced between 1961 and 1962. First exhibited in July 1962 at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles, the works challenged traditional distinctions between fine art and commercial imagery. Warhol focused on commercial packaging rather than the everyday items themselves, which prompted initial controversy but eventual acclaim, and the series catapulted him to fame. The original 32 canvases were preserved by art dealer Irving Blum and acquired by the [[Museum of Modern Art]] in 1996. Two editions of 250 10-print screen print portfolios, issued in 1968 and 1969, are sometimes confused with the original series.

Top professional [[Association football|association football]] league in [[Brazil]], also called the *Brasileirão*. Contested by 20 clubs, it operates promotion and relegation with the Série B. The *Confederação Brasileira de Futebol* (CBF) organized the first national championship in 1971. Since 1959, 156 clubs have played in it, and Palmeiras has won the title 12 times. In 2021 the IFFHS named it the strongest national league in the world.

Waxy, colorless solid with a strong aroma, classified as a terpenoid and [[Ketone|cyclic ketone]]. It is derived from the wood of the camphor laurel (*Cinnamomum camphora*) and from the kapur tree of Southeast Asia. Natural camphor is extracted from wood by steam distillation, and it can also be produced synthetically from [[Turpentine|oil of turpentine]]. Camphor is chiral; the common natural form is (+)-camphor, while the (−)-form is very rare in nature. Doses exceeding 50 mg/kg can be lethal in adults.

Form of [[Recreation|outdoor recreation]] or education involving overnight stays in a basic temporary shelter, such as a [[Tent|tent]]. Campers may also use a recreational vehicle, a cabin, a hammock or no shelter at all. Recreational camping became popular among elites in the early 20th century and later among other socioeconomic classes. Modern campers frequent publicly owned land such as [[National park|national parks]] and state parks, as well as commercial campgrounds. [[Scouting]] and other youth organizations use camping to teach self-reliance and teamwork. The history of recreational camping is often traced to Thomas Hiram Holding, a British traveling tailor. The first commercial camping ground may have been Cunningham's camp near Douglas, Isle of Man, which opened in 1894.

Ancient Semitic-speaking civilization and region of the southern [[Levant]] during the late 2nd millennium BC. In the Late Bronze Age Amarna period (14th century BC), Canaan was an area where the spheres of interest of the [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptian]], Hittite, [[Mitanni]] and [[Assyria|Assyrian]] empires converged or overlapped. The demonym "Canaanites" is a catch-all ethnic term for the indigenous populations of the region, both settled and nomadic-pastoral. Biblical scholar Mark Smith suggests that Israelite culture largely overlapped with and derived from Canaanite culture.

Large [[Goose|goose]] species (*Branta canadensis*) native to the Arctic and temperate regions of [[North America]]. It has a black head and neck, white cheeks and a brown body. It has been introduced to [[France]], the United Kingdom, Ireland, Scandinavia, New Zealand and other regions. Adept at living in human-altered areas, it has established breeding colonies in urban and cultivated habitats, where it is often considered a pest because of its excrement, crop depredation, noise and aggressive territorial behavior.

Canadian public broadcaster and Crown corporation, offering [[Radio|radio]] and [[Television|television]] in English and French as CBC/Radio-Canada. It was established on November 2, 1936, and is the oldest continually existing broadcasting network in Canada. Its funding is supplemented by commercial advertising on its television broadcasts. Its primary radio networks have been commercial-free since 1974. Budget cuts in the early 2010s reduced its service on the airwaves.

Professional [[Canada|Canadian]] football league, the highest professional level of the sport, headquartered in [[Toronto]]. It has nine teams in two divisions. The league was established on January 19, 1958, through the merger of the Interprovincial Rugby Football Union (founded 1907) and the Western Interprovincial Football Union (1936). Its playoffs culminate in the Grey Cup, one of Canada's largest annual sports and television events.

Geologic shield of exposed Precambrian igneous and high-grade metamorphic rock, centered on [[Hudson Bay]] in eastern and central [[Canada]]. It forms the [[North America|North American]] craton, the ancient geologic core of the continent, and its exposed area covers about 8,000,000 sq km (3,100,000 sq mi). Mountains once rose about 12,000 m (39,000 ft) before erosion reduced the region to low relief over some 500 million years. Its rocks date from 2.5 to 4.2 billion years. Glaciation has left a thin layer of soil, and many of Canada's major ore deposits are associated with greenstone belts. The shield also extends south into the northern United States.

[[Spain|Spanish]] archipelago and autonomous community in the [[Atlantic Ocean]], about 100 km (60 mi) off the northwest coast of [[Africa]] (pop., 2025: 2,258,866). The seven main islands are [[Tenerife]], Fuerteventura, Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro. The capitals are Santa Cruz de Tenerife and [[Las Palmas|Las Palmas de Gran Canaria]]. Tourism is a major industry, with over 14.1 million visitors in 2023, drawn by beaches and a subtropical climate. Mount Teide, a [[World Heritage Site]] on Tenerife, is the highest peak in Spain. During the Age of Sail, the islands were the main stopover for Spanish galleons during the colonization of the Americas.

Capital city of [[Australia]] (pop., 2025: 484,630), the country's largest inland city. It was established as a compromise between [[Sydney]] and [[Melbourne]], Australia's two largest cities. The area had been inhabited by [[Aboriginal Australians]] for up to 21,000 years. Canberra was founded and named in 1913, and unusually for an Australian city it was entirely planned to a design by American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin. It is the seat of the federal government, with Parliament House and the High Court.

Resort city in Quintana Roo, southeast [[Mexico]], on the northeast coast of the [[Yucatán Peninsula]]. It lies on the [[Caribbean Sea]] and includes the Hotel Zone, the main tourist area. Cancún was created to foster tourism, and development began on January 23, 1970, when Isla Cancún had only three residents. The Mexican federal government financed the first nine hotels. By 2024 the metropolitan population had reached 1,045,000.

[[International System of Units|SI]] base unit of luminous intensity, symbol cd. It measures the luminous power per unit solid angle emitted in a particular direction. A common wax [[Candle|candle]] gives roughly 1 cd, and the word is Latin for candle. Before 1948, countries used different standards, such as the English candlepower. The 2018 redefinition, effective from May 20, 2019, fixes the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540×10¹² Hz at 683 lm W⁻¹, a frequency in the visible spectrum near green, corresponding to about 555 nm.

American actress and former fashion model. She won five Primetime Emmy Awards and two Golden Globe Awards as the title character in the [[CBS]] sitcom *Murphy Brown* (1988–1998, 2018). Her films include *The Group* (1966) and *Starting Over* (1979), for which she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. She appeared in three episodes of the [[HBO]] series *Sex and the City* (2002–04) and starred in *Boston Legal* (2005–2008) on ABC.

French [[Satire|satirical]] novella by [[Voltaire]], first published in 1759. Its title character, a young man, lives a sheltered life in an Edenic [[Paradise|paradise]] and is taught [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibnizian]] optimism by his mentor, Professor Pangloss. After this life ends, Candide becomes painfully disillusioned as he experiences great hardships. The novella closes with the practical precept "we must cultivate our garden" rather than Pangloss's "all is for the best". Its erratic, fast-moving picaresque plot parodies adventure and romance clichés, and it ridicules religion, governments and philosophers. Many events draw on history, including the [[1755 Lisbon earthquake]]. After its publication the book was widely banned for blasphemy and sedition, but it is now considered Voltaire's *magnum opus*.

Ignitable wick embedded in wax or another flammable solid, such as tallow, that provides light and sometimes fragrance. The word comes from Latin *candēla*, from *candēre* ("to shine"). Candles have been used for over two millennia and were a major indoor light source until other sources were invented. [[Electric light]] has made them largely nonessential for illumination, but they remain common for functional, symbolic and aesthetic purposes. Early beeswax candles were expensive and limited to the elite and churches, and tallow was a cheaper alternative. [[Paraffin wax|Paraffin wax]] made candles affordable for the general public. As the wick burns, heat melts the wax, which vaporizes and combines with [[Oxygen]] to form the flame.

Sweet confection in which sugar is the principal ingredient, also called sweets or lollies. Sugar confectionery includes [[Chocolate]] and chewing gum, and sugar-glazed vegetables, fruit or nuts are considered candied. Before [[Sugar]] was readily available, candy was based on [[Honey]], which was used to coat fruits and flowers. Before the [[Industrial Revolution]], candy was often considered a form of [[Medicine|medicine]], and in the Middle Ages spiced sugar confections were served at banquets as an aid to digestion. From the 1830s technological advances made candy available to working-class people and children, and penny candy became the first good that children bought with their own money. In 1847 the candy press made it possible to produce multiple shapes and sizes at once. High sugar content is associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes and dental caries.

Large terrestrial [[True toad|true toad]] (*Rhinella marina*) native to [[South America]] and mainland [[Central America]]. Adults average 10–15 cm (4–6 in) in length. It was introduced to islands of [[Oceania]] and the [[Caribbean]], and to northern [[Australia]], as a means of pest control against the cane beetle, which damages [[Sugarcane|sugar cane]]. Its toxic skin and tadpoles can kill many animals, and it is particularly dangerous to dogs. It is now considered a pest and an [[Invasive species|invasive species]] in many introduced regions.

Biological family of [[Carnivore|carnivoran]] mammals, from Latin *canis* ("dog"). The family includes the Caninae, the living canids such as [[Wolf|wolves]], [[Coyote|coyotes]], [[Fox|foxes]] and [[Jackal|jackals]], as well as the extinct Borophaginae and Hesperocyoninae. Canids are found on all continents except [[Antarctica]], and range from the 2 m (6.6 ft) gray wolf to the 24 cm (9.4 in) [[Fennec fox|fennec fox]]. Most are social, and typically only the breeding pair in a group breeds, rearing one litter a year in an underground den. The [[Dog|domestic dog]] descends from a symbiotic relationship with Upper Paleolithic humans.

Southern-hemisphere [[Constellation|constellation]], one of the 88 modern constellations. Its name is Latin for "greater dog", and it was included among [[Ptolemy]]'s 48 constellations in the 2nd century. It contains [[Sirius]], the brightest star in the night sky, which appears bright because of its proximity to the [[Solar System]]. In ancient [[Mesopotamia]], Sirius was seen as an arrow aimed at Orion, while the Greeks later depicted it as a dog. The Milky Way passes through the constellation, and the open cluster M41 lies within its borders. The red hypergiant VY CMa is one of the largest stars known.

Genus of 10 species of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] native to the American tropics, known as cannas or canna lilies. Cannas are not true lilies; they belong to the order Zingiberales, together with gingers and bananas. Their large foliage has led horticulturists to develop selected forms as large-flowered garden plants. The flowers are red, orange or yellow and are pollinated by [[Bee|bees]], [[Hummingbird|hummingbirds]], [[Sunbird|sunbirds]] and bats. The rhizomes store starch, having the largest starch grains of all plant life, and cannas are used in agriculture as a source of [[Starch|starch]]. The name Canna comes from the Latin word for a cane or reed.

Genus of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the family Cannabaceae, widely accepted as indigenous to Asia. The number of species is disputed, with as many as three recognized: *Cannabis sativa*, *C. indica* and *C. ruderalis*. It is an annual, dioecious herb, with male and female flowers usually on separate plants. The term [[Hemp|hemp]] usually refers to varieties cultivated for non-drug uses such as fiber, seed oil and textiles. The plant has long been used for medicine and as a [[Cannabis (drug)|recreational drug]], and strains have been bred for high or low levels of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).

Psychoactive drug from the [[Cannabis|cannabis]] plant, also called marijuana, weed, pot or ganja. It is used recreationally and as a medicinal drug, and sometimes for spiritual purposes. Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is its main psychoactive component, and effects include euphoria, altered sense of time, impaired short-term memory and increased appetite. There is a strong relation between cannabis use and the risk of [[Psychosis|psychosis]]. Long-term adverse effects may include addiction, heart disease and chronic coughing. In 2013, between 128 and 232 million people used cannabis, making it the most commonly used largely illegal drug in the world. Uruguay became the first country to legalize recreational use, in 2013, and other countries include [[Canada]], Germany and Thailand.
